games.title: Basics of Biosafety: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which Biosafety Level (BSL) is required for handling dangerous and exotic agents that pose a high individual risk of life-threatening disease, for which there are no available vaccines or treatments?
questions.explanation: BSL-4 is reserved for high-risk, exotic pathogens causing fatal infections without known treatment or vaccines, such as the Ebola virus.

questions.q: A clinical microbiology laboratory is processing sputum samples for suspected Mycobacterium tuberculosis. What is the minimum recommended Biosafety Level for handling these aerosol-transmitted cultures?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an airborne pathogen causing serious disease and requires BSL-3 containment facilities.

questions.q: Immediately after administering an intramuscular injection to a patient, which action is most appropriate to minimize the risk of a needle-stick injury?
options: Recap the needle using both hands before disposal
Dispose of the unsheathed needle immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container
Bend the needle to render it unusable before disposal
Place the needle in a yellow biohazard plastic bag
questions.explanation: Sharps should never be recapped or bent, and must be immediately discarded unsheathed into a dedicated puncture-resistant container to prevent needle-stick injuries.

questions.q: What are the standard operating parameters required for effective sterilization using a gravity displacement autoclave?
questions.explanation: Standard steam autoclaving requires 121°C for 15 to 20 minutes at 15 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure to ensure complete destruction of bacterial endospores.

questions.q: Standard Precautions in infection prevention and control must be applied in which of the following scenarios?
options: Only to patients with confirmed transmissible infections
Only when contact with blood or body fluids containing visible blood is expected
To all patients receiving care, regardless of their diagnosed or presumed infection status
Only when performing invasive surgical procedures
questions.explanation: Standard Precautions are designed to be applied to all patients at all times, regardless of their diagnosis or presumed infection status.

questions.q: Which containment device provides protection to the laboratory worker, the environment, AND the sample product through HEPA-filtered laminar airflow?
questions.explanation: Class II Biosafety Cabinets protect the worker, environment, and sample product using HEPA-filtered laminar airflow.

questions.q: A medical student sustains a contaminated needle-stick injury while drawing blood from a patient with unknown infectious status. What is the immediate first step in post-exposure management?
options: Squeeze the puncture site vigorously to express blood
Wash the exposure site thoroughly with soap and water
Apply a tight tourniquet proximal to the puncture site
questions.explanation: The immediate initial action following a skin puncture exposure is to wash the wound gently with soap and water without scrubbing or squeezing.

questions.q: According to standard biohazard waste color-coding guidelines, which container should be used for infectious non-sharp biological waste such as soiled dressings and gloves?
questions.explanation: Yellow containers or bags are used universally for infectious biohazardous waste intended for autoclaving or incineration.

questions.q: A biological agent that can cause human disease and poses a moderate individual hazard, but a low risk to the community, with effective treatment available, belongs to which Risk Group?
questions.explanation: Risk Group 2 includes pathogens that present moderate individual risk and low community risk, with effective treatments or preventive measures available.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes sterilization from disinfection?
options: Sterilization destroys all microorganisms including bacterial endospores, whereas disinfection reduces pathogenic organisms but may not eliminate spores
Disinfection eliminates all forms of microbial life including endospores, whereas sterilization only reduces the vegetative bacterial load
Sterilization applies only to living tissue, whereas disinfection applies to inanimate objects
Disinfection requires high-pressure steam, whereas sterilization relies solely on low-level chemical agents
questions.explanation: Sterilization completely eliminates all microbial life including bacterial spores, whereas disinfection eliminates most recognized pathogenic microorganisms except bacterial spores.

games.title: Hepatitis: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A neonate is born to a mother who is Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) positive and Hepatitis B e-antigen (HBeAg) positive. What is the most appropriate initial management for the infant within 12 hours of birth?
options: Hepatitis B vaccine and Hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG)
questions.explanation: Infants born to HBeAg-positive mothers should receive both the Hepatitis B vaccine and Hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth to prevent vertical transmission.

questions.q: A 7-year-old girl presents with fatigue, jaundice, and elevated liver transaminases. Serological testing reveals positive anti-liver kidney microsomal type 1 (anti-LKM1) antibodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune hepatitis type 2 predominantly affects children and is defined by the presence of anti-LKM1 antibodies.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with acute onset hepatitis, Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, and dysarthria. Which laboratory finding best supports a diagnosis of Wilson's disease?
options: Absent urinary copper after penicillamine challenge
questions.explanation: Wilson's disease typically presents with reduced serum ceruloplasmin levels accompanied by elevated urinary copper excretion.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with low-grade fever, nausea, and jaundice following an outbreak at a daycare center. Serology confirms acute Hepatitis A virus (HAV) infection. What is the most expected long-term outcome for this patient?
options: High risk of progression to chronic hepatitis
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A in young children is almost always self-limiting and leads to full recovery with lifelong immunity without causing chronic liver disease.

questions.q: A 2-month-old infant presents with prolonged jaundice, pale stools, and hepatomegaly. A liver biopsy reveals periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive, diastase-resistant cytoplasmic granules within hepatocytes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency characteristically demonstrates periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive, diastase-resistant inclusions in hepatocytes on histopathology.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with jaundice and acute encephalopathy. Which lab finding is required to meet the diagnostic criteria for paediatric acute liver failure (PALF)?
options: Coagulopathy unresponsive to Vitamin K (INR > 1.5 with encephalopathy or > 2.0 without)
questions.explanation: Paediatric acute liver failure is primarily defined by biochemical liver injury paired with uncorrected coagulopathy.

questions.q: A 14-year-old adolescent presents 6 hours after an intentional overdose of paracetamol with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and nausea. What is the definitive initial antidote?
questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine is the primary antidote for paracetamol toxicity as it restores hepatic glutathione stores required to detoxify toxic metabolites.

questions.q: A 10-year-old child undergoing routine pre-chemotherapy screening has positive Hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) and negative Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and core antibody (anti-HBc). How should these serological results be interpreted?
questions.explanation: Isolated anti-HBs positivity with negative anti-HBc and HBsAg confirms effective immunity derived from Hepatitis B vaccination.

questions.q: A 2-week-old breastfed infant presents with lethargy, poor feeding, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and bilateral nuclear cataracts. A urine test is positive for reducing substances. Which enzyme deficiency causes this condition?
questions.explanation: Classic galactosemia is caused by a deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (GALT), presenting with early infant liver dysfunction, cataracts, and Escherichia coli sepsis.

questions.q: An infant is born to a mother with chronic Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. At what age should non-PCR antibody screening be performed in the infant to definitively determine their HCV status?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C antibody testing in exposed infants is delayed until 18 months of age to allow time for transplacentally acquired maternal antibodies to clear.

games.title: Acute Abdomen and Appendicitis: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a 12-hour history of periumbilical pain that has migrated to the right lower quadrant, accompanied by anorexia and low-grade fever. On examination, he has focal tenderness at McBurney's point with rebound tenderness and a positive Rovsing's sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant associated with McBurney's point tenderness and Rovsing's sign is classic for acute appendicitis.

questions.q: A 26-year-old pregnant woman (20 weeks gestation) presents with right-sided abdominal pain, low-grade fever, and mild leukocytosis. Physical examination reveals localized tenderness in the right flank, but graded compression ultrasonography of the right lower quadrant is inconclusive due to the gravid uterus. What is the next best diagnostic step?
options: Abdominal CT scan with intravenous contrast
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen
questions.explanation: MRI without contrast is the preferred next imaging modality for suspected appendicitis in pregnant patients when ultrasound is inconclusive.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female presents with a 5-day history of progressively worsening lower abdominal pain, high fever (38.9°C), and systemic inflammatory signs. Abdominal CT demonstrates a 5 cm fluid collection with a peripheral enhancing rim and extraluminal air in the pelvis adjacent to a retrocecal appendix. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Initial management of a stable patient with a localized, large appendiceal abscess (>3-4 cm) is percutaneous drainage accompanied by intravenous antibiotics.

questions.q: A 68-year-old male presents with a 2-day history of left lower quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and altered bowel habits. Physical examination shows localized left lower quadrant tenderness and guarding, and lab work reveals leukocytosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Left lower quadrant pain, fever, altered bowel habits, and leukocytosis in an older adult are classic features of acute sigmoid diverticulitis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with a history of chronic NSAID use presents with sudden-onset, severe, generalized abdominal pain that began 2 hours ago. On examination, his abdomen is rigid and board-like with severe generalized tenderness and absence of bowel sounds. What is the initial diagnostic test of choice to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An upright chest radiograph is the initial test to detect pneumoperitoneum (free air under the diaphragm) caused by a perforated hollow viscus.

questions.q: A 23-year-old female presents with bilateral lower abdominal pain, purulent vaginal discharge, and dyspareunia for 3 days. On pelvic examination, there is marked cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lower abdominal pain accompanied by purulent vaginal discharge and cervical motion tenderness (Chandelier sign) strongly indicates pelvic inflammatory disease.

questions.q: A 74-year-old female with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden, severe diffuse abdominal pain out of proportion to physical examination findings. Abdominal examination reveals mild diffuse tenderness without peritoneal signs, while arterial blood gas shows severe metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Severe abdominal pain disproportionate to physical exam findings in a patient with atrial fibrillation, combined with lactic acidosis, is characteristic of acute mesenteric ischemia.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with right lower quadrant pain and low-grade fever. Abdominal palpation reveals deep right lower quadrant tenderness without prominent anterior rebound, but passive extension of the right hip reproduces severe right lower quadrant abdominal pain. Which physical exam sign is positive in this patient?
questions.explanation: Pain elicited by passive extension of the right hip is a positive Psoas sign, indicating irritation of the psoas muscle commonly seen in retrocecal appendicitis.

games.title: Anemia: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 45-year-old female presents with severe fatigue, craving for ice, and brittle, spoon-shaped nails. Complete blood count reveals Hb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, and serum iron studies show low ferritin with an elevated total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Microcytic anemia accompanied by low serum ferritin, elevated TIBC, and classic symptoms like pica indicates iron deficiency anemia.

questions.q: A 62-year-old male presents with progressive fatigue, a smooth beefy tongue, and tingling in his lower extremities. Laboratory testing shows Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, and elevated serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic anemia accompanied by subacute combined degeneration symptoms (neuropathy) and elevated methylmalonic acid is characteristic of vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.q: A 24-year-old male presents with jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue two days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Peripheral blood smear reveals Heinz bodies and bite cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute intravascular hemolysis triggered by oxidative medications, featuring Heinz bodies and bite cells on blood smear, is classic for G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: A 38-year-old female with systemic lupus erythematosus presents with shortness of breath, scleral icterus, and mild splenomegaly. Hb is 7.1 g/dL, reticulocyte count is 6%, and the direct Coombs test (DAT) is strongly positive for IgG. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Extravascular hemolysis in the setting of autoimmune disease with a direct Coombs test positive for IgG indicates warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

questions.q: A 58-year-old male with stage 4 chronic kidney disease presents for follow-up with worsening lethargy. CBC reveals Hb 8.8 g/dL, MCV 86 fL, and normal iron saturation, while serum erythropoietin levels are markedly low. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Normocytic anemia caused by decreased erythropoietin synthesis in chronic kidney disease is treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents once iron deficiency is ruled out.

questions.q: A 29-year-old female presents with mucosal bleeding, easy bruising, severe fatigue, and recurrent bacterial fever. CBC shows Hb 6.5 g/dL, absolute neutrophil count 300/µL, and platelets 12,000/µL, while bone marrow biopsy demonstrates marked hypocellularity replaced by fat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Severe pancytopenia paired with a hypocellular bone marrow dominated by adipocytes confirms the diagnosis of aplastic anemia.

questions.q: An asymptomatic 26-year-old male of Mediterranean descent undergoes routine blood testing showing Hb 11.5 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, an elevated red cell count, and normal serum ferritin. Hemoglobin electrophoresis reveals an HbA2 level of 4.8%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Microcytosis out of proportion to mild anemia with elevated red blood cell count and high HbA2 on electrophoresis is diagnostic of beta-thalassemia minor.

questions.q: An 18-year-old male with sickle cell disease presents to the emergency department with severe, deep aching pain in his back and lower extremities. Hb is 7.5 g/dL (baseline 7.8 g/dL), oxygen saturation is 97% on room air, and he has no fever or pulmonary infiltrates. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation: Uncomplicated acute vaso-occlusive pain crisis in sickle cell disease is managed supportively with aggressive intravenous fluids and prompt opioid analgesia.

games.title: Prefrontal Association Areas: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Atomoxetine is used in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) to improve executive functioning mediated by the prefrontal cortex. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Selective inhibition of the presynaptic norepinephrine transporter (NET)
Direct agonism at dopamine D2 receptors
Irreversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase type B (MAO-B)
questions.explanation: Atomoxetine acts as a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (NET inhibitor), increasing both norepinephrine and dopamine concentrations in the prefrontal cortex.

questions.q: Guanfacine improves prefrontal cortex-mediated working memory and impulse control in patients with ADHD. Which receptor subtype does guanfacine selectively stimulate in the prefrontal cortex?
questions.explanation: Guanfacine is a selective post-synaptic alpha-2A adrenergic receptor agonist that strengthens prefrontal cortical network connectivity and improves executive function.

questions.q: Methylphenidate is a first-line psychostimulant that enhances focus and executive function controlled by the prefrontal association cortex. How does it alter monoamine levels in this region?
options: Stimulates direct postsynaptic release of serotonin
Blocks dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake via DAT and NET inhibition
Acts as a selective 5-HT1A receptor partial agonist
questions.explanation: Methylphenidate increases extracellular dopamine and norepinephrine in the prefrontal cortex primarily by blocking the dopamine transporter (DAT) and norepinephrine transporter (NET).

questions.q: In schizophrenia, prefrontal cortex hypofunction is associated with cognitive deficits and negative symptoms. Which receptor action of second-generation antipsychotics like clozapine helps increase dopamine release in the prefrontal cortex?
questions.explanation: Antagonism of prefrontal 5-HT2A receptors disinhibits local dopamine release, which helps alleviate negative and cognitive symptoms associated with prefrontal hypofunction.

questions.q: Donepezil is prescribed to slow cognitive decline affecting prefrontal association networks in Alzheimer's disease. What is its main mechanism of action?
questions.explanation: Donepezil works by reversibly inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, thereby increasing synaptic acetylcholine levels in cortical regions, including the prefrontal association area.

questions.q: Bupropion is an antidepressant that modulates prefrontal circuit activity involved in motivation and concentration. What is its pharmacological class?
questions.explanation: Bupropion acts as a norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor (NDRI), raising catecholamine levels in prefrontal pathways.

questions.q: Glutamatergic excitotoxicity in cortical association areas contributes to cognitive decline in neurodegenerative dementias. Which mechanism describes how memantine protects prefrontal neurons from glutamate-induced damage?
options: Uncompetitive low-affinity NMDA receptor channel blockade
High-affinity blockade of L-type voltage-gated calcium channels
questions.explanation: Memantine acts as an uncompetitive, low-affinity NMDA receptor antagonist, preventing pathological tonic glutamate excitotoxicity while preserving physiological neurotransmission.

questions.q: Modafinil enhances prefrontal cortex activation to promote wakefulness and executive function. What is a primary FDA-approved clinical indication for modafinil?
questions.explanation: Modafinil is primarily indicated for promoting wakefulness in conditions such as narcolepsy, shift work sleep disorder, and obstructive sleep apnea.

games.title: Surgical Management in Year 4: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man undergoing elective colorectal surgery receives intravenous metronidazole preoperatively. What is the primary mechanism of action of metronidazole?
options: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
Disruption of bacterial DNA via formation of toxic reactive intermediates
Inhibition of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is reduced within susceptible anaerobic organisms to form toxic intermediates that cause DNA strand breakage and cell death.

questions.q: A patient undergoing an emergency laparotomy receives succinylcholine (suxamethonium) for rapid sequence induction. Which electrolyte abnormality is a recognized, potentially life-threatening adverse effect of this medication?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine causes sustained depolarization of the motor endplate, triggering an efflux of intracellular potassium that can lead to acute hyperkalemia.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman in the post-anaesthesia care unit is given IV ondansetron for severe nausea following abdominal surgery. What is the mechanism of action of ondansetron?
questions.explanation: Ondansetron selectively blocks 5-HT3 receptors both peripherally on vagal nerve terminals and centrally in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.

questions.q: Sugammadex is administered postoperatively to rapidly reverse neuromuscular blockade. Which agent does sugammadex directly bind and encapsulate to achieve this effect?
questions.explanation: Sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that selectively encapsulates aminosteroid neuromuscular blocking drugs, predominantly rocuronium and vecuronium.

questions.q: A post-surgical patient is prescribed low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Potentiation of antithrombin III with selective inhibition of Factor Xa over Factor IIa
Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase
questions.explanation: Enoxaparin binds antithrombin III to cause a conformational change that preferentially accelerates the inactivation of Factor Xa relative to Factor IIa.

questions.q: Propofol is commonly used for both the induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia in major surgery. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A receptors
questions.explanation: Propofol produces sedation and anaesthesia primarily by potentiating GABA-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission through GABA-A receptors.

questions.q: Bupivacaine is widely used for regional nerve blocks and epidural anaesthesia. Which systemic toxic effect is most characteristically associated with accidental intravascular injection of bupivacaine?
options: Severe cardiotoxicity and refractory ventricular arrhythmias
questions.explanation: Bupivacaine is highly lipophilic and dissociates slowly from cardiac sodium channels, making accidental intravascular entry prone to causing severe cardiotoxicity and malignant arrhythmias.

questions.q: Tranexamic acid is routinely administered perioperatively in orthopedic and trauma surgery to reduce blood loss. What is its mechanism of action?
options: Direct enzymatic conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin
questions.explanation: Tranexamic acid is a synthetic lysine analogue that competitively inhibits the binding of plasminogen to fibrin, thereby inhibiting fibrinolysis and stabilizing blood clots.
